content_html:
The Homunculus Problem

The homunculus problem highlights a regress in theories that explain perception or memory via internal representations. If there is an “inner picture,” who is the inner observer that interprets it? Any such observer would need its own representations, leading to infinite regress.

A regress challenge for representational theories of mind and memory.

Representation = internal picture or symbol.
Problem: for the picture to mean something, a “viewer” must exist inside the head.

This viewer would itself require another viewer → infinite regress. The regress exposes the flaw in naïve “inner cinema” theories. This challenges representationalism and simplistic computational theories because it forces clarification of how representations are used, not “watched.”

Applies to memory: avoids picturing it as a “mental movie.”

  • Use without user: representations guide processes, not an inner spectator.
  • Distributed processing: perception/memory emerge from networks, no central observer.
  • Enactivism/Direct Realism: reject inner pictures; mind is world-involving activity.

If memory were a stored movie, regress arises: who watches the memory? Instead:

Pattern reinstatement
Reconstruction, not playback
Embodied re-engagement

This clarifies levels of explanation: neurons don’t “see pictures.” Mind = systemic use of information, not inner viewing. An AI analogy: models don’t “read” symbols — they process them functionally.
